summaries.example: Imagine two actions that are exactly alike in every ordinary way: the same choice, the same reason, the same results, and the same situation. It would be strange to say that one action is right while the other is wrong, with no other difference at all. Ethical supervenience is the idea that an ethical difference needs some other difference to go with it.
summaries.summary: Ethical supervenience is a philosophical idea about how ethical differences are connected to other differences. If two possible actions or situations match in all the relevant non-ethical ways, the idea says they cannot differ ethically without some further difference. For example, if two acts had the same setting, intentions, actions, and consequences, it would be puzzling to call one wrong and the other acceptable for no additional reason. Philosophers disagree about what the relevant underlying features are. Some discuss natural features; others use the broader idea of all non-ethical features. Using all features would make the claim uninteresting, because an ethical difference would already count as a difference. Philosophers also distinguish different forms of supervenience. A claim may compare individual things, whole possible worlds, or the judgments people make. It may be weaker or stronger depending on which kinds of possibilities it covers. Some thinkers regard the connection as built into ethical concepts. Others think it is a fact about reality, nature, or special ethical principles. Still others question whether the connection is as strong as it first seems. The entry examines these choices and asks whether ethical supervenience can support arguments about realism, reduction, ethical knowledge, and moral principles.
key_ideas: Ethical supervenience says that two perfectly alike situations cannot differ ethically for no reason at all.
Philosophers ask what ethical properties depend on: natural facts, non-ethical facts, or something else.
They also ask how strong the connection is and whether it concerns things themselves or our judgments.
Supervenience describes a pattern of connection, but by itself it does not explain why the pattern holds.
summaries.why_it_matters: This idea helps philosophers ask what ethical thinking is committed to. It can challenge a view that says two completely alike cases may have different ethical statuses for no reason. It also helps separate several questions: what makes something right or wrong, how we know that, and whether ethical facts are real. Studying supervenience shows why a simple-sounding claim can hide many different theories.

important_terms.definition: A pattern in which one kind of difference cannot happen without some other kind of difference.
A feature that tells us whether something is right, wrong, good, or bad.
The features that help explain an ethical judgment, such as what someone did and what happened afterward.
A complete way things might be, including all the facts about a whole universe.

questions_to_think_about: If two choices had exactly the same facts around them, could one be right and the other wrong?
What facts might make an action wrong: its results, its purpose, or something else?
Does saying that ethical differences need other differences explain enough?
Could people agree that two cases must be judged alike even if they disagree about whether the cases are actually right or wrong?

summaries.example: Consider two possible actions that match in every base respect: the agent’s motives, the physical and social circumstances, the action itself, the trust involved, and all short- and long-term effects. One might initially think that one action could be wrong while its duplicate is permissible. Yet that possibility seems difficult to understand. Ethical supervenience captures the thought that an ethical difference requires some difference in the base facts. The philosophical question is whether this intuition establishes only a conceptual constraint on ethical judgment or a stronger metaphysical fact about reality.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the claim that ethical properties cannot vary without corresponding variation in some base properties. This is not one thesis but a family of theses. The base may be natural properties, non-ethical properties, descriptive properties, or—trivially—all properties. The structure may concern individuals or complete possible worlds. Weak supervenience permits different possible worlds to associate ethical properties with different base patterns; strong supervenience rules out that kind of variation, while global supervenience is formulated in terms of world-wide distributions. The strength of the modal claim is also unsettled. Ethical supervenience might be logical, conceptual, nomic, metaphysical, or normative, and these modalities are not interchangeable. A further distinction separates ontological claims about ethical properties from ascriptive claims about the correctness of ethical judgments. The standard motivation combines case-based intuition with a ban on brute ethical contingency: unlike some physical facts, ethical patterns should not simply happen without explanation. Yet the source surveys objections. Conceivability may not reliably reveal possibility, and the apparent force of the thesis may depend on controversial views about language, concepts, or modality. Supervenience arguments have been used against realism and non-reductive realism, while realist theories have appealed to reduction, functional realization, grounding, analytic facts, or ethical laws to explain the covariance. Anti-realists may explain ascriptive supervenience through the practical function or consistency of ethical discourse, but this may not explain ontological supervenience. Finally, even if supervenience is true, its dialectical importance is disputed: an unclear base
key_ideas: The base question asks what ethical properties supervene on. Natural properties are a common proposal, but the notions of natural and non-ethical are disputed.
Structural versions differ: individual, global, weak, strong, and intuitive formulations do not make identical commitments.
Modal strength matters. Logical, conceptual, nomic, metaphysical, and normative necessity describe different kinds of impossibility.
Ontological supervenience concerns properties; ascriptive supervenience concerns whether ethical judgments are mistaken.
Arguments for supervenience often generalize from particular cases and reject unexplained ethical variation, but critics question both the inference and its explanatory value.
Supervenience alone does not establish reduction, realism, or a complete ethical principle; additional premises are needed.
summaries.why_it_matters: Supervenience sits between everyday moral reasoning and highly abstract metaphysics. It expresses the intuition that ethical judgments should not change arbitrarily while everything else stays fixed. At the same time, it does not by itself tell us whether morality is natural, non-natural, realist, anti-realist, reducible, or grounded in principles. Understanding that limitation prevents philosophers from treating one covariance claim as a complete theory of ethics.

important_terms.definition: A covariation relation: differences in one class of properties require differences in another class, without this relation itself explaining why.
Properties such as being right, wrong, good, virtuous, or otherwise ethically significant.
The properties on which the supervening properties are said to depend in their pattern of variation.
A supervenience claim about properties possessed by particular entities or actions rather than entire worlds.
A claim that complete possible worlds with the same distribution of base properties also share the same distribution of ethical properties.
A weaker form allowing ethical patterns to vary between possible worlds, provided each world has a stable ethical pattern.
A stronger form requiring the relevant covariation across all metaphysically possible cases.
A judgment-centered claim that treating apparently base-identical cases differently is a mistake, without directly committing to ethical properties.

questions_to_think_about: Would a strong metaphysical supervenience thesis make ethical properties reducible to base properties, or can necessary covariance fall short of identity?
Is the inability to imagine an ethical difference without a factual difference evidence about concepts, reality, or merely our habits of thought?
Could an ascriptive supervenience claim be accepted by someone who denies that ethical properties exist?
Does a highly complicated base condition count as an ethical principle if it predicts every case but explains none?
What would a theory need to add to supervenience in order to explain why a particular action is wrong?

summaries.example: Suppose two students copy the same answers, for the same reason, under the same conditions, and the copying produces the same effects. It seems odd to say that copying is wrong in one case but not wrong in the other while insisting that there is no other difference. Ethical supervenience is the idea that an ethical difference must come with some difference in the facts. The hard part is deciding which facts count.
summaries.summary: Ethical supervenience is the claim that ethical differences cannot appear without differences in other relevant features. If two actions or situations are alike in all the base respects, they should not differ ethically for no further reason. Philosophers use this idea in several different ways. They debate whether the base consists of natural properties, all non-ethical properties, descriptive properties, or something more carefully defined. They also distinguish claims about individual cases from claims about complete possible worlds. Weak supervenience allows the ethical pattern to differ between worlds, while strong supervenience requires a tighter connection. Another issue is the kind of necessity involved. A connection might be true because of meanings, the laws of nature, the nature of reality, or ethical standards. These possibilities have different consequences. The entry also separates ontological supervenience, which concerns ethical properties, from ascriptive supervenience, which says that judging apparently identical cases differently is a mistake. Many arguments for supervenience begin with particular examples and generalize from them. They also appeal to the thought that ethical facts should not be unexplained accidents. Other philosophers argue that our intuitions may not show genuine impossibility, or that supervenience has little explanatory power. The idea has been used in debates over ethical realism, reduction, anti-realism, moral knowledge, and the existence of general moral principles. But supervenience alone does not settle these debates. A theory must still explain what the base is, why the connection holds, and what kind of necessity it involves.
key_ideas: Philosophers do not agree on what the ethical supervenes on. “Natural” may be too narrow or unclear, while “all properties” may be too easy and uninformative.
Supervenience can compare individual cases or entire possible worlds.
Weak and strong supervenience differ over whether ethical rules could vary from one possible world to another.
The connection may be conceptual, metaphysical, natural-law-based, or normative.
Ascriptive supervenience focuses on judgments and may be available even to philosophers who reject ethical properties.
Supporters see supervenience as a way to rule out arbitrary ethical differences; critics question whether it really explains anything.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept helps us test whether a moral theory treats similar cases consistently. It also shows why philosophical disagreements can continue even after people accept the same starting intuition. Two thinkers may agree that ethical differences need factual differences but disagree about which facts matter, whether the connection is necessary, and whether it describes reality or only good judgment. That makes supervenience a useful map of questions rather than a final answer.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a change in ethical status requires a change in some other relevant features.
A feature that makes something ethically important, such as being wrong, fair, kind, or harmful.
The underlying non-ethical features used to compare cases, such as actions, motives, or consequences.
A complete way a universe could be, not merely a small situation.
A version of supervenience about whether things or actions have properties.
A version about whether a person makes a mistake by judging two apparently alike cases differently.
A weaker connection that can allow different ethical rules in different possible worlds.
A stronger connection that keeps the ethical pattern fixed across the relevant possible cases.

questions_to_think_about: If two cases look alike in every ordinary fact, what kind of hidden difference could justify different ethical judgments?
Would a rule that lists every possible case be a real ethical principle, or just a huge description?
Can someone believe that ethical judgments must fit together consistently without believing that ethical properties exist?
Is “it is impossible” clear enough, or should we ask whether the impossibility is logical, conceptual, physical, or metaphysical?
Why might a philosopher want ethical differences to have explanations rather than be accidental?
